y-m-81-01.title: If you stack fifths twelve times, do you land on an octave?
y-m-81-01.topic: Music and Math: Interval Ratios and Equal Temperament
y-m-81-01.goal: Treat musical intervals as frequency ratios, explain with odd and even numbers why stacking just fifths never meets an octave exactly, and compare what 12-tone equal temperament gives up as a compromise.
y-m-81-01.material: The pitch of a note is given by its frequency (how many times it vibrates per second). If the frequency ratio of two notes is 2:1, they are one octave apart and have the same note name. If it is 3:2, the interval is called a 'just perfect fifth.' Stacking intervals means multiplying the frequency ratios again and again. If you go up 12 just fifths from a starting note, you arrive at a pitch close to the note with the same name 7 octaves above the starting note. Assumption: every fifth has a ratio of exactly 3:2, and an octave is exactly 2:1.
y-m-81-01.thinking.0: Judging by telling 'similar' apart from 'exactly equal'
y-m-81-01.thinking.1: Adjusting how sure you are after seeing a new calculation result
y-m-81-01.thinking.2: Comparing what the two methods gain and what they give up
y-m-81-01.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-01.prereq.1: Calculating exponents (powers), multiplying fractions, properties of odd and even numbers
y-m-81-01.prereq.2: No music knowledge is needed: intervals are explained as frequency ratios.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.prompt: The materials are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your thought about this question: 'Is the note you get by stacking 12 fifths exactly the same pitch as the note with the same name 7 octaves higher?'
y-m-81-01.s.s1.hint.0: Separate what you can say with the information you have now from what you still need to calculate or work out.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether each choice says 'the pitches are similar' or 'the frequency ratios are exactly equal.'
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Stacking two fifths multiplies the frequency by (3/2)×(3/2)=9/4 (nine fourths). Since multiplying by 2 is an octave, dropping one octave gives 9/8. In the same way, we want to compare the note stacked 12 times with the note 7 octaves up (128 times, which is 2 multiplied 7 times).
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Do you think (3/2) to the 12th power, the value after stacking 12 times, is exactly equal to 128?
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.after: You can check by calculating, or you can look for a reason in the structure of multiplication. 'The pitches are close, so they are equal' is not enough evidence yet.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The pitches match up this closely, so it must be exactly equal to 128.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: A feeling that the pitches are similar is different from a claim that the ratios are exactly equal. You need to check with a calculation or a reason.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Powers of 3 are odd, so they can never equal powers of 2.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You built a reason from the structure of multiplication (odd and even). You can also ask whether this reason works for every number of stacks.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: You can't decide whether they are equal or different until you calculate and compare with 128.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You did not jump to a conclusion without evidence, and you thought of a way to check. After calculating, keep going by judging from the result.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Calculating gives (3/2) to the 12th power = 531441/4096 ≈ 129.746. Since 2 to the 7th power is 128, the ratio is 129.746÷128 ≈ 1.0136 (about 1.4% higher).
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Which statement fits this result best?
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.after: We have confirmed that it does not match at 12 stacks, but this one calculation cannot tell us about other numbers of stacks. That is why we need a step to find a reason.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It did not match at the 12th stack. Whether it fails for other numbers of stacks too, we need to work out with a reason.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You separated what is confirmed (12 stacks) from what is not yet known (other numbers of stacks). How to close that gap is the next question.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The difference is only 1.4%, so in math too we can treat them as equal.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even if they sound similar to the ear, claiming they are 'exactly equal' is a different matter. The small difference is still there.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: If we stack more, at some number of stacks it will become exactly equal to a power of 128.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: That is an expectation with no evidence. You need to try other numbers of stacks or build a reason.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is a rounding error from turning a fraction into a decimal, so it is really equal to 128.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: 531441/4096 is an exact fraction. The difference cannot be explained by rounding error.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.info: If (3/2) to the n-th power equals 2 to the m-th power, then 3 to the n-th power = 2 to the (m+n)-th power. If n is 1 or more, the left side is odd and the right side is even. So no matter how many fifths you stack, you never get exactly some number of octaves. The 12-tone equal temperament used on keyboard instruments sets the fifth to 2 to the 7/12 power (about 1.4983) instead of 3/2, so that 12 stacks make exactly 2 to the 7th power.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does 12-tone equal temperament deal with this problem?
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.after: 3/2 (1.5) and 2 to the 7/12 power (about 1.4983) differ by about 0.11%. 12-tone equal temperament is a compromise: it gives up a very little on the fifth so that the result of 12 stacks matches the octaves exactly.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Keep the just fifth 3:2 as it is, and narrow the octave a little to make it fit.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: In 12-tone equal temperament the octave is also kept at 2:1. Look again at what was changed to make it fit.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Increase the notes from 12 to 53 so that there is no error at all.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 12-tone equal temperament uses 12 notes. This explanation does not mention changing the number of notes.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Set the fifth a little narrower than 3:2, so that 12 stacks make exactly 7 octaves.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You read carefully what is kept fixed and what is given up. You can also check how small the amount given up is.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Do not use fifths at all and build the 12 notes from other intervals only.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: 12-tone equal temperament also has fifths. Notice that their ratio is very close to 3/2.
y-m-81-01.s.s1.reflect: What evidence did you use for your first judgment, and how did your confidence in it change after seeing the calculation and the odd-even reason? In what situations do 'almost equal' and 'exactly equal' lead to different conclusions?
y-m-81-01.s.s2.prompt: Compare the method that keeps the just fifth (3:2) with the 12-tone equal temperament method, and write one thing each gains and one thing each gives up.
y-m-81-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write side by side what happens to 'the ratio of a fifth' and 'the result of 12 stacks' in each method.
y-m-81-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write a sentence that pairs one thing gained with one thing given up in return.
y-m-81-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Do the 'gain' and the 'give-up' you wrote point to different methods?
y-m-81-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write 'slightly off' concretely, using the ratios (3/2 versus about 1.4983) or the result of 12 stacks if possible?
y-m-81-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Instead of writing that one method is always better, did you think that the choice can change depending on what you put first?
y-m-81-01.s.s2.model.0: A just fifth has a ratio of exactly 3:2, so the two notes blend cleanly, but 12 stacks do not line up with the octaves, so the pitches change when you change key. In 12-tone equal temperament, the fifth is made a little narrower than 3:2 so that 12 stacks make exactly 7 octaves; you can use the same keys in every key, but the fifth differs very slightly from the just fifth.
y-m-81-01.s.s2.model.1: If you keep the just fifth, the ratio is exactly 3:2, but after going all the way around the twelve notes you don't match the starting note. Equal temperament gives every fifth the same ratio, 2 to the 7/12 power, so it gains a perfect round trip, and at the cost of drifting a little from 3:2.
y-m-81-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: I summarized it as what is gained and what is lost, not as 'which one is better.'

y-m-81-02.title: Let's design a leap year rule ourselves
y-m-81-02.topic: The Calendar and Leap Year Rules
y-m-81-02.goal: Understand that the leap year rule sets the average length of a year, design several rules that meet the conditions, and compare and explain the sizes of their errors.
y-m-81-02.material: The time the Earth takes to go once around the Sun (the tropical year) is about 365.2422 days. A calendar year is 365 days or 366 days (a leap year), so we have to decide every how many years to add a day. We write a rule as 'insert L leap days in a cycle of N years,' and the average year is 365+L÷N days. Assumption: take the tropical year to be 365.2422 days, and compare how far the calendar drifts from the seasons by the difference in the averages.
y-m-81-02.thinking.0: Estimating how big the building-up drift gets
y-m-81-02.thinking.2: Finding the error in a description of a rule
y-m-81-02.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-02.prereq.1: Calculating with decimals and fractions, the idea of an average, multiples and remainders (divisors and multiples)
y-m-81-02.prereq.2: The value of about 365.2422 days for the tropical year (the time the Earth takes to go once around the Sun) is given in the material.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.prompt: Estimate first. If you only use a leap year once every 4 years (adding one day every 4 years) and keep going, roughly how far will the calendar drift from the seasons after 1000 years?
y-m-81-02.s.s1.hint.0: For the 4-year rule, write the average length of a year next to 365.2422 days and compare them.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what happens when a small yearly difference builds up 1000 times.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.a: You may have taken the yearly difference as too small, or lost a place value when multiplying by the number of years.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.b: You took the yearly difference to be about 10 times too big. Write down again the difference between the average length under the 4-year rule and 365.2422 days.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.o.c: About 8 days (a little over a week)
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.c: You gauged the size by multiplying the small difference that builds up each year by the number of years.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.o.d: It doesn't drift (because there are leap years).
y-m-81-02.s.s1.r.d: Even with leap years, if the average is not exactly equal to the tropical year, the difference builds up. Compare the averages.
y-m-81-02.s.s1.explain: The average of the 4-year rule is 365.25 days and the tropical year is about 365.2422 days, so a difference of 0.0078 days builds up each year. After 1000 years that is about 7.8 days, so roughly 8 days.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.prompt: Now design one yourself. For the rule 'insert L leap days in a cycle of N years,' make 2 different rules whose yearly average (365+L÷N days) is within 0.0005 days of 365.2422 days. (N is a natural number up to 400, and L is an integer 0 or more.)
y-m-81-02.s.s2.hint.0: In the average 365+L÷N, L÷N needs to be close to 0.2422. First choose N, then change L and compare L÷N.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.hint.1: Try it to see whether a small N or a large N makes it easier to fit the error within the allowed range.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.ok.c1: N and L are integers within the conditions.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.fail.c1: N must be an integer from 1 to 400, and L must be an integer 0 or more.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The average year is close to 365.2422 days.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The average year is off from 365.2422 days by more than 0.0005 days.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.explain: Examples: 8 days in 33 years (average about 365.2424 days), 31 days in 128 years (average 365.2421875 days), and 97 days in 400 years (average 365.2425 days) all satisfy the condition. Rules with the same ratio L÷N (for example 8 days in 33 years and 16 days in 66 years) count as the same rule. There are many other rules that fit the condition.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain, using numbers at least once, why the rule you chose drifts from the seasons less than 'a leap year every 4 years.'
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the average of your rule and the average of the 4-year rule (365.25) each with 365.2422.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write the difference that builds up each year for the two rules side by side.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the drift of your rule and of the 4-year rule on the same basis (the yearly average, or after a few hundred years)?
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Instead of only writing 'more accurate,' did you show evidence with two or more numbers?
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.model.0: My rule has 97 days in 400 years, so the average is 365.2425 days, which differs from 365.2422 by 0.0003 days. The 4-year rule has an average of 365.25 days, so it drifts 0.0078 days every year, which means my rule drifts much less.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.model.1: With 8 days in 33 years, the yearly average is about 365.2424 days, so the error is about 0.0002 days. That is much smaller than the 4-year rule's error of 0.0078 days, so even after 1000 years it drifts by less than a day.
y-m-81-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: I even added a numerical estimate that it is less than a day after 1000 years.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.prompt: This is a text that explains the leap year rule used in many countries now. Which line has something wrong?
y-m-81-02.s.s3.hint.0: Apply lines 1 to 3 in order to the year 2000 and see which line applies last.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check one by one whether the three years in line 4 meet the condition in line 3.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.0: A year divisible by 4 is a leap year.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.1: However, a year divisible by 100 is not a leap year.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.2: However, a year divisible by 400 is a leap year again.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.3: Therefore 1900, 2000, and 2100 are all multiples of 100, so they are common years.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.line.4: Under this rule, 97 leap days are inserted in 400 years, so the yearly average is 365.2425 days.
y-m-81-02.s.s3.explain: Line 4 is wrong. The year 2000 is a multiple of 100, but it is also a multiple of 400, so by line 3 it is a leap year. 1900 and 2100 are common years. Line 5 is correct: in 400 years, subtract the 4 multiples of 100 from the 100 multiples of 4 and add the 1 multiple of 400, and you get 97.

y-m-81-03.title: Throwing yut sticks: is every result equally likely?
y-m-81-03.topic: Probability in the Traditional Game Yut
y-m-81-03.goal: Tell the number of outcomes apart from equal likelihood, judge how the comparison of the probabilities of yut and mo changes when new data and conditions are given, and say what information is needed.
y-m-81-03.material: In the game of yut, you throw 4 yut sticks at once, and the result is decided by how many sticks land with the flat side (the belly) up. 1 belly is do, 2 is gae, 3 is geol, 4 is yut, and 0 (all round backs) is mo. Assumption: the sticks are thrown without affecting each other (independent), and the probability that one stick lands belly up is p. For real yut sticks, p depends on how they are made.
y-m-81-03.thinking.0: Finding the line where the error starts
y-m-81-03.thinking.1: Adjusting your judgment and confidence after seeing new data
y-m-81-03.thinking.2: Pointing out the information needed for a conclusion
y-m-81-03.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-03.prereq.1: Counting cases (the product rule), the product of probabilities of independent events, percentages and ratios
y-m-81-03.prereq.2: Even if you have never played yut, you can solve this using only the rules explained in the material.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.prompt: A student explained the probabilities of throwing yut sticks like this. Assume the probability p that one stick lands belly (flat side) up is 1/2. In which line does the first wrong statement appear?
y-m-81-03.s.s1.hint.0: Label the sticks ①②③④ and list how many of the 16 patterns have exactly 1 belly.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count in a table how many of the 16 patterns each of do, gae, geol, yut, and mo corresponds to, and compare them.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.0: There are five kinds of results: do, gae, geol, yut, and mo.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.1: The patterns of 4 sticks showing belly or back are 2×2×2×2=16, and if p=1/2, all 16 of these patterns are equally likely.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.2: But there are five results, so each result is equally likely.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.line.3: So the probability of yut is 1/5, and the probability of mo is also 1/5.
y-m-81-03.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong first in line 3. Having 5 results does not make them equally likely. Of the 16 patterns, do (1 belly) has 4, gae has 6, geol has 4, and yut and mo have 1 each, so the probabilities are 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16, 1/16. Line 4 is a conclusion that follows from the wrong statement in line 3.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.prompt: The materials are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your thought about this question: 'Which comes up more often, yut (all 4 bellies) or mo (all 4 backs)?'
y-m-81-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how surely the information given now tells you the value of p.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write the probability of yut and the probability of mo by splitting them into each stick's belly probability and back probability.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.info: All 4 sticks are ideal yut sticks with p=1/2. Among the 16 patterns, yut is 1 pattern (all bellies) and mo is also 1 pattern (all backs).
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.ask: Which comes up more often, yut or mo?
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.after: If p=1/2, yut and mo are both 1/16, so they are equal. But real yut sticks may not have p exactly equal to 1/2.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.o.a: Yut comes up more often. It is more natural for the belly to face up.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.r.a: You said p=1/2, so belly and back are equally likely. This reason does not fit the given assumption.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.o.b: Mo comes up more often. Mo moves you far, so it probably is harder.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.r.b: A big score and a small probability are different things. Under this assumption, you should compare by the number of patterns.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.o.c: Both results are 1 pattern out of 16, so they come up equally often.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.0.r.c: You compared by counting the number of patterns. This comparison relies on the assumption that p=1/2.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.info: You threw one real yut stick 100 times, and the belly came up 60 times (assume all four sticks have the same shape).
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.ask: What do you think about yut and mo after seeing this data?
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.after: The chance of getting 60 or more out of 100 when p=1/2 is about 3%. It is not common, but not impossible, so whether you think p is greater than 0.5 or keep your first judgment, it is reasonable as long as you state your evidence. If p=0.6, yut is about 0.130 and mo is about 0.026, so yut is about 5 times as likely.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.a: It was 60, so we can fix p=0.6, and we can say that yut comes up about 5 times as often as mo.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.a: 100 throws is not a large number. 0.6 is an estimate, not a fixed value, and it could be 0.55 or 0.65.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.b: p could be around 0.6, so yut may come up more often than mo. But be careful about how much more often.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.b: You also mentioned the uncertainty in the estimate. Your judgment links the amount of data to your confidence.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.c: The belly came up 60 times and the back 40 times, so the ratio of yut to mo is also 60:40, about 1.5 times.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.c: For yut, all four sticks must show belly, so it is p multiplied four times. You cannot use the ratio of one stick as it is.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.o.d: 60 out of 100 can happen by chance, so there is still little reason to give up the first judgment that p=1/2.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.1.r.d: You considered the range that chance can explain and kept your first judgment. You can also think about how far from that range it becomes hard to call it chance.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.info: The four sticks are different from each other: two sticks have a belly probability of 0.6, and the other two have a belly probability of 0.4 (the sticks do not affect each other).
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.ask: Which comes up more often, yut or mo?
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.after: Yut is 0.6×0.6×0.4×0.4=0.0576 and mo is 0.4×0.4×0.6×0.6=0.0576, so they are equal. When the p of all the sticks is the same, yut and mo are equal only when p=1/2, but when each stick is different, they can happen to be equal like this.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.o.a: Yut comes up more often, because some sticks have a belly probability of 0.6.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.a: There are sticks with 0.6, but there are also sticks with 0.4. Write the probabilities of yut and mo each as a product and compare them.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.o.b: It cannot be decided from only the condition that the sticks do not affect each other.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.b: With the condition 'they do not affect each other,' you can multiply the probabilities. Check again whether the values you need are already given.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.o.c: Mo comes up more often, because some sticks have a low belly probability.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.c: For mo, you also have to consider that the stick with 0.6 lands on its back with probability 0.4.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.o.d: They are equal. Yut is 0.6×0.6×0.4×0.4 and mo is 0.4×0.4×0.6×0.6, so the products are the same.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.st.2.r.d: You compared yut and mo by writing each as a product. You noticed that the same numbers are used in both, with the sticks showing belly on one side and back on the other.
y-m-81-03.s.s2.reflect: How did your judgment when p=1/2 change after the 100-throw data and after learning that p differs from stick to stick? Say whether the new information changed your judgment or changed how sure you are.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.prompt: To say 'yut and mo are equally likely,' what more information is needed, and how could you compare once you have it? Write it.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side how each stick must land for yut and how each must land for mo.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.hint.1: Think about which values you need to know to compare the two with numbers.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: First I need to know ...
y-m-81-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the information you wrote really used to calculate the probability of yut and the probability of mo?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also think about whether the sticks affect each other (independence)?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you tell apart 'when all the p are the same' and 'when each stick is different'?
y-m-81-03.s.s3.model.0: You need to know the probability p that each stick lands belly up. If all four sticks have the same p, yut and mo are equal only when p=1/2; if each stick is different, you must compare the product of each stick's belly probabilities with the product of their back probabilities.
y-m-81-03.s.s3.model.1: You need to know each stick's probability of landing belly up and whether the sticks affect each other (independence). With those values, multiply all the belly probabilities for yut and all the back probabilities for mo, and compare.

y-m-81-04.title: Does a check digit catch every mistake?
y-m-81-04.topic: The Check Digit in Book Numbers
y-m-81-04.goal: Show with counterexamples that a check digit always catches a one-digit mistake but can miss a swap of neighboring digits, and say what 'passing' guarantees.
y-m-81-04.material: A book number (ISBN-13) is a 13-digit number with a 'check digit' at the end. Rule: multiply the 1st digit from the left by 1, the 2nd by 3, the 3rd by 1, the 4th by 3, and so on, alternating. If the sum of all 13 products is a multiple of 10, the number is accepted as correct. People make mistakes when copying numbers, so let's look at which mistakes this method catches. Assumption: exactly one mistake happens, and it is either (A) one digit is replaced by a different digit, or (B) two neighboring digits are swapped.
y-m-81-04.thinking.2: Judging how far a conclusion is guaranteed
y-m-81-04.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-04.prereq.1: Remainders (the remainder after dividing by 10), adding and multiplying integers, expressions with letters
y-m-81-04.prereq.2: The method for computing the check digit is in the material (students who don't know it can still solve this).
y-m-81-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose your first judgment. How does this check method handle (A) a mistake where one digit is replaced by another digit, and (B) a mistake where two neighboring digits are swapped?
y-m-81-04.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one digit and write how much the sum changes when it is replaced by another digit.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.hint.1: Pick two digits and calculate how much the sum changes when two neighboring digits are swapped.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.o.a: There are cases that neither (A) nor (B) can catch.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.r.a: For (A), notice that the multiplier is 1 or 3. If one digit changes, how much does the sum change?
y-m-81-04.s.s1.o.b: (A) is always caught, but (B) is sometimes missed.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.r.b: You noticed that the sum changes in different ways for the two kinds of mistakes. The key is that the two neighboring positions have different multipliers.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.r.c: Whether the sum changes depends on the multiplier and the size of the change. Two neighboring positions have different multipliers.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.o.d: (B) is always caught, but (A) is sometimes missed.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.r.d: Work out what condition is needed for the difference between the sums before and after to be a multiple of 10.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.explain: If one digit changes, the sum changes by (multiplier)×(size of the change). With a multiplier of 1 or 3 and a change of 1 to 9, this can never be a multiple of 10. When two neighboring digits are swapped, the sum changes by 2×(difference of the two digits), so when the difference is 5 it becomes a multiple of 10 and is missed.
y-m-81-04.s.s1.acc.0: As a prediction before checking, that is possible. Whether there are pairs in (B) whose change in the sum is a multiple of 10 is something you can test directly in the next step.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.prompt: For two neighboring digits, call the front digit a (multiplier 1) and the back digit b (multiplier 3). Make 3 different pairs where a and b are different digits and swapping them leaves the ones digit of the total sum unchanged (so the check misses it). (A pair with a and b swapped counts as the same pair.)
y-m-81-04.s.s2.hint.0: Plug in a few pairs and compare whether the ones digits of a+3×b (as is) and b+3×a (swapped) are the same.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.hint.1: Collect in a table the pairs that gave the same ones digit and look for what they have in common.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are single digits from 0 to 9.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from 0 to 9.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.fail.c2: If a and b are the same, nothing was swapped.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The ones digit of the sum is the same before and after swapping.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The ones digit of the sum is different before and after swapping, so the check catches it.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.explain: (0,5), (1,6), (2,7), (3,8), (4,9) and the pairs with their order swapped all satisfy the condition. In every one, the difference of the two digits is 5.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Find and write what the pairs you made have in common, and explain why that does not change the ones digit of the sum.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write your pairs in one line, and find the relationship between the two digits (difference, sum, product, and so on) for each.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write the difference between the sum before swapping and the sum after swapping in terms of a and b.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: My pairs are ..., and what they have in common is ...
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does what they have in common fit all the pairs you made?
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the common feature does not change the ones digit of the sum, or did you only observe it?
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.model.0: (0,5), (1,6), (2,7) all have a difference of 5 between the two digits. Swapping changes the sum by 2×5=10, and 10 does not change the ones digit, so the check misses it.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.model.1: The pairs I found are 0 and 5, 4 and 9, and 3 and 8, and subtracting the smaller from the larger always gives 5. Swapping makes the sum go down or up by 10, so the ones digit stays the same.
y-m-81-04.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: I wrote both the observation and the reason.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.prompt: A number passed the check. Can you be sure this number has no copying mistakes at all?
y-m-81-04.s.s3.hint.0: Think about whether a number made by swapping the pair you just made would pass the check.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about the case where one place changes by +1 and another by −1 (when the two places have the same multiplier).
y-m-81-04.s.s3.o.a: You cannot be sure. There are mistakes that get missed, so it can pass anyway.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.r.a: You thought about what passing guarantees. The pairs from the earlier step show that there really are kinds of mistakes that get missed.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.o.b: You can be sure. Passing the check means there is no mistake.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.r.b: Passing the check only means 'none of the kinds of mistakes that get caught happened.' You just made examples of mistakes that are not caught.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.o.c: You can be sure, but only when the number is very long, like 13 digits.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.r.c: A longer length does not make the missed mistakes go away. The pairs that get missed have nothing to do with length.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.o.d: You cannot be sure. In fact, numbers that pass have more mistakes.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.r.d: Passing does not increase the number of mistakes. Being able to miss something is different from having more mistakes.
y-m-81-04.s.s3.explain: Passing the check only means 'none of the mistakes this check can catch happened.' It misses a swap of neighboring digits that differ by 5, and it can also pass when two or more places are wrong and the changes in the sum cancel each other out.

y-m-81-05.title: How many Hangul syllables have no final consonant?
y-m-81-05.goal: Tell apart the ratio of possible shapes from the ratio actually used in real writing, and say what information and methods are needed to find the latter.
y-m-81-05.material: One syllable of modern Hangul is made of an initial consonant, a medial vowel, and, if there is one, a final consonant (batchim). The agreement for this task: count 19 choices for the initial consonant, 21 for the vowel, and 28 for the final consonant, including 'no final consonant.' Assumption: any initial, vowel, and final can be freely paired, and we count the shapes that can be made. We do not consider whether those syllables are actually used.
y-m-81-05.thinking.0: Estimating a ratio with the product rule
y-m-81-05.thinking.1: Telling possible cases apart from how often they are actually used
y-m-81-05.thinking.2: Pointing out the information needed for a conclusion
y-m-81-05.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-05.prereq.1: Multiplying numbers of cases, fractions and percentages
y-m-81-05.prereq.2: Being able to read the names of the Hangul letters (the explanation that a syllable is made of an initial, a vowel, and a final is in the material)
y-m-81-05.s.s1.prompt: Estimate. Among all the shapes that can be made, roughly what fraction are syllables without a final consonant?
y-m-81-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the number of all syllables without a final consonant and of all syllables with a final consonant, each in terms of the numbers of initials, vowels, and finals.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.hint.1: When you find the ratio of the two counts, look at what happens to the numbers of initials and vowels.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.a: 'No final' is 1 out of the 28 choices for the final. Count again what fraction of the whole 1 out of 28 is.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.b: Taking the share of 'no final' among the 28 finals to be one fourth is too big. The initial and vowel are multiplied in the same way in every case.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.c: It seems you split it into just two groups, 'has a final' and 'has no final,' and saw it as half and half. The cases with a final split into 27 kinds.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.r.d: You compared the number of cases with no final to the total number of cases. You used the fact that the numbers of initials and vowels go into both sides in the same way.
y-m-81-05.s.s1.explain: Syllables with no final number 19×21=399, and the total is 19×21×28=11172. The ratio is 399÷11172=1/28≈3.6%. The numbers of initials and vowels are multiplied in the same way whether or not there is a final, so the ratio becomes 1 out of the 28 finals.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.prompt: Seeing the about 3.6% found above, a student said, "Then in real writing too, only about 3.6% of the syllables will have no final." What about this statement?
y-m-81-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether 'the number of possible shapes' and 'the number of times they appear in writing' are the same thing.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what conclusion you would get if every syllable appeared the same number of times, and whether that assumption would be true.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.a: Yes. It is the ratio among all possible syllables, so it is the same ratio in writing too.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.a: The ratio of 'possible shapes' and the ratio of 'syllables actually used' are different. It depends on how often each syllable is used.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.b: No. You need to know how often each syllable is used in writing.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.b: You separated the number of possible shapes from the number of times they are actually used. You saw the frequency of use as information that has to be looked up separately.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.c: No. But if the text gets very long, it will naturally come close to 3.6%.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.c: The value that settles down as the text gets longer is the ratio used in the text. It does not move toward the ratio of the number of possible shapes.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.o.d: We can't know. The information that there are 28 kinds of finals might be wrong.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.r.d: The 28 kinds is the agreement of this task. The question is not the agreed number but whether you may turn a ratio of counts into a frequency of use.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.explain: 11172 is the number of 'shapes that can be used.' In real writing, some syllables are used very often and some are hardly used. Without the assumption that every shape is used equally often, you cannot turn a ratio of counts into a ratio of use.
y-m-81-05.s.s2.acc.0: You can say that if you assume every syllable is used with the same frequency. But whether that assumption is true in real writing has to be checked separately.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.prompt: How would you find out the ratio of syllables with no final in real writing? Write the method and at least one limit of that method.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one text to read and think of a way to sort its syllables into two groups (no final / has a final).
y-m-81-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether the result can be trusted when you pick only one text.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both how you choose the text and the process of making a ratio from the counted results?
y-m-81-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: When you wrote the limit, did you point out specifically 'what this method cannot tell you'?
y-m-81-05.s.s3.model.0: Pick one text, count the syllables with no final, and divide by the total number of syllables to get the ratio. But one text can be lopsided by chance, so you should collect several texts and count the same way to trust it.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.model.1: Pick one page of a book, count the syllables with no final and the total syllables, and find the ratio. One page can differ by the kind of writing, so you should collect and compare many kinds of writing, such as poems and explanatory texts.
y-m-81-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: I gave as a limit that the result depends on the kind of writing.

y-m-81-06.title: If one vertex works, does the whole pattern work?
y-m-81-06.topic: Regular Polygon Patterns and Tiling the Plane
y-m-81-06.goal: Find several combinations whose angles at one vertex add to 360°, and judge that this condition is not enough to fill the whole plane.
y-m-81-06.material: When making a pattern, you join regular polygon tiles with no gaps and no overlaps. The angles of the tiles meeting at one vertex must add up to 360°. The size of one angle of a regular n-gon is set by n (a regular triangle 60°, a regular square 90°, a regular hexagon 120°). In this task we only look at the case where three regular polygons meet at one vertex, and the number of sides is a natural number from 3 to 50.
y-m-81-06.thinking.1: Finding different combinations that meet the constraints
y-m-81-06.thinking.2: Telling necessary conditions from sufficient conditions
y-m-81-06.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-06.prereq.1: The size of an interior angle of a regular polygon (middle school geometry), solving fractions and equations
y-m-81-06.prereq.2: An intuition for regular polygons surrounding a point (angles adding up to a full turn)
y-m-81-06.s.s1.prompt: Guess first. Besides three regular hexagons (6,6,6), what other combinations of three regular polygons at one vertex have angles adding to 360°? (An n-gon has n sides, and n is at most 50.)
y-m-81-06.s.s1.hint.0: If there is one regular triangle (60°), think about what the sum of the other two polygons' angles must be.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.hint.1: Use the same method when there is one regular square (90°), and find a few combinations.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.a: Regular polygons other than the regular triangle, square, and hexagon (such as the regular octagon) also have angles. What if you test one or two of them?
y-m-81-06.s.s1.o.b: There are only a few combinations that include a regular triangle.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.b: Also check whether there are combinations without a regular triangle. What about sums that include a regular pentagon or a regular octagon?
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.c: You left open that polygons other than regular triangles, squares, and hexagons can be used. You can test directly to check the number.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.r.d: It is hard to find a reason that there is only one more. Count directly how many combinations you can make with polygons other than the regular triangle, square, and hexagon.
y-m-81-06.s.s1.explain: If you look for them yourself in the next step, you will find that there are 10 combinations in all, including (6,6,6).
y-m-81-06.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 4 different combinations in which a regular a-gon, a regular b-gon, and a regular c-gon meet at one vertex and the angles add to exactly 360°. (3 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ 50, all natural numbers. Count a combination with a different order as the same one.)
y-m-81-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table of the size of one angle of a regular n-gon and write down a few starting from 3.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.hint.1: Pick the smallest a, find what the sum of the other two angles must be, and then change b.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of sides are natural numbers from 3 to 50.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of sides must be natural numbers from 3 to 50.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.ok.c2: You entered them in the order a ≤ b ≤ c.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Please enter them in the order a ≤ b ≤ c.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The three angles add up to exactly 360°.
y-m-81-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The three angles do not add up to 360°.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.prompt: Look at (5,5,10) among the combinations you found. At one vertex, two regular pentagons and one regular decagon can fill 360°. Then can this combination alone make a pattern that fills the whole plane with no gaps?
y-m-81-06.s.s3.hint.0: Draw the vertices of the neighboring shapes around one side of the regular decagon and check whether the same combination continues.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.hint.1: When two regular pentagons meet along a side, check whether the neighboring vertex also gives the same combination.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.a: One point matching is not enough to know. You have to check separately that the neighboring vertices match too.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.a: You separated matching at one point from matching everywhere. You sorted out what is a necessary condition and what is a sufficient condition.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.b: Only (4,6,12), the combination that uses all three kinds, can fill the whole plane with no gaps.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.b: (6,6,6) and (4,8,8) also have patterns that fill the whole plane. The number of kinds is not the criterion.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.c: The angles at one vertex add up correctly, so continuing in the same way will always fill the whole plane.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.c: The angles at one point adding up correctly is a necessary condition. Whether the neighboring vertices also work with the same combination is a separate matter.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.o.d: The number of combinations that work at one vertex is always equal to the number of patterns that fill the plane.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.r.d: The question is whether every combination fills the whole plane. There is no reason the number of combinations and the number of patterns are equal.
y-m-81-06.s.s3.explain: The angles at one vertex adding to 360° is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. As far as is known, of the 10 above, only (3,12,12), (4,6,12), (4,8,8), and (6,6,6) fill the whole plane with one kind of vertex arrangement, and (5,5,10) cannot fill the whole plane because continuing to the neighboring vertices leads to a contradiction.

y-m-81-07.title: After how many years does the sexagenary name come around again?
y-m-81-07.goal: Judge that some pairs never appear when the heavenly stems and earthly branches move together, and explain, by correcting an error and finding several answers, how the repeating cycle is set by the relationship between the two cycles.
y-m-81-07.material: In the traditional calendar, each year is named by pairing one of the 10 heavenly stems (갑·을·병·정·무·기·경·신·임·계) with one of the 12 earthly branches (자·축·인·묘·진·사·오·미·신·유·술·해). When the year changes, both the stem and the branch move one step to the next name, and when they reach the end they return to the start. The names of the first six years are 갑자, 을축, 병인, 정묘, 무진, 기사. (This is only a way of naming in the calendar. It has nothing to do with fortune-telling, and we look at it only as a rule of numbers.)
y-m-81-07.thinking.0: Judging an impossible case from the rule
y-m-81-07.thinking.2: Finding several values that meet the constraints and explaining how they are related
y-m-81-07.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a label for the difficulty and support level of this production batch. It does not mean that any subject is assigned to any grade. The 'Math and Culture' topic is assumed to be tackled by students who have already learned high school math (numbers, expressions, functions, and simple probability).
y-m-81-07.prereq.1: Divisors and multiples, the meaning of the least common multiple (middle school level), remainders
y-m-81-07.prereq.2: You can solve this using only the rule in the material, even without knowing the names of the stems and branches.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.prompt: If you keep naming the years by the rule above, will there be a year with the name '갑축,' in which the stem '갑' is paired with the branch '축'?
y-m-81-07.s.s1.hint.0: For the first six years, number the stems and the branches (starting from 1) and write them side by side.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many steps the branch moves before the same stem comes up again.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.o.a: Yes. All 120 pairs of the 10 stems and 12 branches appear in some year.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.r.a: Look at the pairs that appeared in the first six years (갑자, 을축, 병인, ...) and see how the branch paired with 갑 moves along.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.o.b: We can't know. Six years are not enough to know the reason, so we have to write out more years.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.r.b: You admitted the data is not enough and tried to write out more. You can also look for the reason in the rule itself.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.o.c: Yes. There are 12 branches that could pair with 갑, so 축 must come up at least once.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.r.c: First you need to check that all 12 branches really pair with 갑. Write how the branch changes in the years when 갑 comes up.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.o.d: No. The stem and the branch move together, so the branches that can pair with 갑 are limited.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.r.d: You thought of why the pairing is limited by the rule. You can check it by seeing how the branch changes in the years when 갑 comes up.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.explain: 갑 comes up every 10 years, and each time the branch moves 10 steps, so counting from 1 it pairs only with the odd-numbered branches (자·인·진·오·신·술), as in 갑자, 갑술, 갑신, 갑오, 갑진, 갑인. 축 is the 2nd branch, so it can't pair with 갑. So there is no 갑축, and the pairs that appear number 60, not 120.
y-m-81-07.s.s1.acc.0: It is reasonable to want to write out more years, since the first six years are hard to settle on. But if you look at the reason in the rule (both move one step together), you can answer without writing out more.
y-m-81-07.s.s2.prompt: A student explained 'when a year with both the stem and branch the same as the first 갑자 year comes again' like this. Which line is wrong?
y-m-81-07.s.s2.hint.0: List the years when each returns to its starting place every 10 years and every 12 years (10, 20, 30, ... and 12, 24, 36, ...), and find the first year they overlap.
y-m-81-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the overlapping year you found comes before the 120 years in line 4.
y-m-81-07.s.s2.line.1: Every year both move one step together, so for 갑자 to come again, both the stem and the branch must return to their starting places.
y-m-81-07.s.s2.line.2: The stem returns to its starting place every 10 years, and the branch every 12 years.
y-m-81-07.s.s2.line.3: So the first time both return to the start at the same time is after 10×12=120 years.
y-m-81-07.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is wrong. They do return after 120 years, but the 'first' time they return is after 60 years. This is because the smallest number that is both a multiple of 10 and a multiple of 12 is 60.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.prompt: Find every case where the name of the year d years after the first 갑자 year is '갑자' again. (1 ≤ d ≤ 200, d is a natural number) Enter 3 different values of d.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.hint.0: List a few values of d where the stem comes back and a few where the branch comes back.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.hint.1: From the two lists you wrote, pick the d that are in both.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.ok.c1: d is a natural number from 1 to 200.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.fail.c1: d must be a natural number from 1 to 200.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.ok.c2: The stem returns to its starting place.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.fail.c2: The stem does not return to its starting place.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.ok.c3: The branch returns to its starting place.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.fail.c3: The branch does not return to its starting place.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.explain: They are 60, 120, and 180. All are multiples of 60, and after 10 years only the stem matches, and after 12 years only the branch matches.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain why 10 years or 12 years later does not work, and how the answers you found are related to each other.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write what happens to the stem and the branch after 10 years and after 12 years.
y-m-81-07.s.s3.because.hint.1: Look at what the d values you found have in common, or the gaps between them.
